confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress; 1 further work by the same author (or citing it for stress) agrees.
catalog_quote: 2.5. Stress. With minor exceptions, stress is predictable and therefore non-phonemic. Stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the word, whether it is a root or a derivation. The only exceptions are certain vowel sequences (see 2.6) and words containing the clitic -a (see 9.22). Secondary stress can be heard on the fourth and sixth syllable from the end; stress therefore seems to be spread out…

audit.reasoning: Quote confirmed verbatim at the stated place (van den Berg 1989 §2.5 p. 25) in the PDF and text we hold; the cross-referenced exceptions (§2.6 pp. 26-27, ch. 3 pp. 42-43 on clitic -a) were read and are minor/lexical, consistent with 'fixed-strict' penult with alternating secondaries (stress placement coded per word length as 10 010 1010 01010 (1 = a stressed syllable) matches 'secondary stress on the fourth and sixth syllable from the end'). The deciding source is the standard xvi+376 pp reference grammar, the best description Glottolog lists; the author's 2004 southern-dialect sketch (downloaded from ANU, p. 135) independently states 'penultimate stress' for the other dialect. Two open recent phonology papers downloaded are silent. Only un-held candidate is Sidu 1996 (Indonesian, print-only), low priority. sources.quote: p. 25, section 2.5: "With minor exceptions, stress is predictable and therefore non-phonemic. Stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the word, whether it is a root or a derivation. The only exceptions are certain vowel sequences (see 2.6) and words containing the clitic -a (see 9.22). Secondary stress can be heard on the fourth and sixth syllable from the end; stress therefore seems to be spread out evenly over the word in rhythmic patterns." Examples on the same page: `ani 'bee'; `bhosu 'w

tone.quote: The basic facts of standard Muna phonology can be given in the following overview (I will use the now generally accepted Muna alphabet and not phonetic symbols): 1) There are five vowel phonemes: i, e, a, o, u. 2) There are twenty-five basic consonants [...] 3) There are no syllable-final consonants; the only occurring syllable types are V and CV. 4) Sequences of two or three vowels are common (each vowel filling a syllable slot). 5) Stress is almost invariably penultimate. 6) The majority of roots are disyllabic, but trisyllabic roots are also common.

tone.quote: Tak kalah pentingnya dalam analisis fonologi ini adalah unsur-unsur prosodi yang berada diatas segmen dan suku kata yang kita kenal dengan suprasegmental, yaitu titinada suara dan intonasi yang termasuk di dalamnya panjang (length) dan tekanan (stress). Jika ada dua vokal yang berbeda pada posisi berdampingan, tekanan (stress) terletak pada suku kata pertama. ... Lain halnya jika ada dua fonem vokal yang sama atau identik pada posisi berdampingan, maka fonem tersebut menjadi fonem vokal panjang.
tone.translation: No less important in this phonological analysis are the prosodic elements above the segment and syllable known as suprasegmentals, namely voice pitch and intonation, including length and stress. If two different vowels are adjacent, the stress lies on the first syllable. ... It is different if two identical vowel phonemes are adjacent: then they become a long vowel phoneme.
tone.summary: Swadesh-list phoneme inventory of Muna; the suprasegmental paragraph names pitch and intonation only generically, no tone or pitch contrast claimed; stress stated only for unlike vowel sequences.

tone.quote: Firstly, no acoustic analysis of the phonemes is given. Secondly, intonation is largely ignored (except when clearly contrastive). [...] 2.5. Stress. With minor exceptions, stress is predictable and therefore non-phonemic. Stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the word, whether it is a root or a derivation. [...] Yes-no questions in Muna are formed simply by use of interrogative intonation. On the basis of their intonation, two types of yes-no questions can be distinguished: a neutral question and a leading question. In the neutral pattern a mid-high head is followed by a rising nucleus [...] The second type of yes-no question is a leading question, in which only the nucleus is spoken on a high tone followed by a mid tone
